item.title: Chinese, Tanzanian educators join forces to boost Chinese language education
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
Chinese, Tanzanian educators join forces to boost Chinese language education Tanzanian Chinese language teacher Gloria Mshana explains Chinese grammar to students in front of the blackboard at the Confucius Institute at the University of Dar es Salaam in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, Oct. 1, 2026. As the world prepares to mark World Teachers' Day on Oct. 5, Chinese and Tanzanian educators are joining forces to expand Chinese language education in Tanzania, blending native linguistic expertise with localized cultural insights. (Xinhua/Emmanuel Herman) DAR ES SALAAM, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- As the world prepares to mark World Teachers' Day on Oct. 5, Chinese and Tanzanian educators are joining forces to expand Chinese language education in Tanzania, blending native linguistic expertise with localized cultural insights. For Gloria Mshana, a Tanzanian teacher, teaching Chinese goes far beyond explaining vocabulary and grammar. It involves connecting an unfamiliar language to local experiences. When teaching about the four seasons, Mshana draws on her firsthand experience of living in China to describe spring, summer, autumn, and winter to Tanzanian students, who are less familiar with such distinct seasonal changes. However, maximizing classroom impact requires a truly collaborative approach. When introducing Chinese cuisine, for instance, native Chinese teachers explain the nuances and cultural background of culinary terms. Mshana then follows up with pictures, videos, and relatable examples, bridging the gap between Chinese traditions and Tanzanian hospitality. This localized approach highlights the strength of the bilateral teaching partnership. While Chinese instructors provide professional linguistic expertise, their Tanzanian colleagues help bridge communication barriers, particularly for beginners fluent in Kiswahili. For Liu Mu, a Chinese volunteer teacher at Ardhi University, a teaching center under the Confucius Institute at the University of Dar es Salaam (CI-UDSM), such cooperation has proved vital. Managing 350 students in her second year, Liu relied on local colleagues to better understand their learning habits. This seamless daily collaboration is reinforced through the institute's regular pedagogical exchanges, such as weekly joint workshops held every Wednesday afternoon to address classroom challenges. Xu Qian, Chinese director of CI-UDSM, noted that the institute's current faculty, comprising seven local Tanzanian teachers, six Chinese teachers, and 18 Chinese volunteers, is a key strength, enabling a highly complementary teaching model. "Chinese teachers bring linguistic expertise and professional training, while Tanzanian teachers deeply understand the local context, students' learning habits and specific challenges," Xu said. Driven by strong demand, enrollment at the institute has soared to roughly six times its pre-2020 levels, with registered learners exceeding 1,000 this year. The impact also extends beyond universities. Masudi Jumanne Kidaso, a 36-year-old teacher at African Prestige Primary School, is currently a beginner-level Chinese learner himself, but he aspires to introduce the language to his own pupils. Encouraged by his Chinese instructors, Kidaso is now developing an introductory textbook for children, using songs, games, and language clubs to teach basic conversations. "I believe this project will help more Tanzanian children begin learning Chinese at an early stage," Kidaso said. Through daily interaction, these educators are sharing knowledge, adapting teaching methods to local needs, and helping students navigate cultural differences. As interest in the Chinese language grows across Tanzania, their collaboration is broadening access to the language while opening doors for future educational, professional, and cultural exchanges. item.title: UN official highlights GDI's role in advancing sustainable development
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
UN official highlights GDI's role in advancing sustainable development Dima Al-Khatib (L, Front), director of the UN Office for South-South Cooperation, speaks at a high-level panel discussion on South-South cooperation, at the UN headquarters in New York, on Sept. 12, 2024. (Xinhua/Xie E) UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- Five years after China proposed the Global Development Initiative (GDI), its focus is shifting increasingly towards practical cooperation that addresses the priorities of developing countries, a senior UN official has said. "Five years on, the Global Development Initiative is showing how shared ambition can translate into practical support for development," Dima Al-Khatib, director of the United Nations Office for South-South Cooperation (UNOSSC), told Xinhua in a written interview. The initiative, she said, has "provided a platform for mobilizing partnerships, knowledge and resources in support of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development." According to a United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) China publication, more than 600 projects under the Global Development Project Pool had been implemented or were in progress by the end of 2024. The associated Global Development Capital Pool had mobilized 14 billion U.S. dollars in financing commitments as of March 2025. "These mechanisms illustrate how cooperation under the GDI is supporting development financing and implementation," Al-Khatib said. An aerial drone photo taken on Sept. 29, 2025 shows the Beni Nadji raw water pre-treatment station project in the Trarza region, Mauritania. (Power Construction Corporation of China/Handout via Xinhua) Al-Khatib pointed to China's longstanding cooperation with UNOSSC, which spans more than two decades. "The strength of South-South cooperation lies in helping countries turn each other's experience into solutions that work for their own communities," she said. One example is the Global South-South Development Center Project, which entered its second phase in 2025 under the China-United Nations Global South-South Development Facility. Working with the China International Center for Economic and Technical Exchanges, the project aims to strengthen a network of more than 60 technical institutions to facilitate cooperation among developing countries. In West Africa, a rice initiative involving the World Food Programme, the African Union and other partners combines technology and training to improve agricultural productivity, reduce post-harvest losses and support rural livelihoods. She also highlighted cooperation on digital development, including e-commerce training that reached participants from more than 90 countries, followed by field studies in China for policymakers from 22 developing countries. With just four years left to meet the 2030 deadline, Al-Khatib said the GDI can support accelerated Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) implementation by connecting nationally identified priorities with technologies, technical expertise, financing and capacity development. A business manager of Hunan Modern Agriculture International Development Co. Ltd checks the growing condition of chili peppers with a local staff member at the Gashora Farm in Nyagatare district, Rwanda, May 22, 2025. (Xinhua/Ji Li) In September 2025, China and the United Nations announced the China-UN Global South-South Development Facility, with 10 million dollars in budget support for the 2025-2030 period. Established under the United Nations Fund for South-South Cooperation, the facility supports cooperation under the GDI in areas, including agriculture, technology and digital development, according to UNOSSC. Al-Khatib said the facility's first call for proposals, which concluded in August, attracted 107 proposals from 16 UN agencies and entities, covering 115 countries across the Global South. "The next phase may prioritize country ownership, measurable results and the adaptation and scaling of solutions suited to local circumstances," she said. Looking ahead, Al-Khatib emphasized the importance of aligning cooperation with the SDGs, UN social and environmental standards, and UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Frameworks. "The objective is to enable developing countries to adapt, co-create and sustain solutions, and share their experience across the Global South, guided by the commitment to leave no one behind," she said. item.title: China upholds principles, promotes dialogue at G20 trade ministers' meeting: commerce ministry
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
China upholds principles, promotes dialogue at G20 trade ministers' meeting: commerce ministry BEIJING, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- China played an active role in promoting dialogue and cooperation with other G20 members while upholding principles during the recent G20 trade ministers' meeting, the country's Ministry of Commerce said on Sunday. The ministry spokesperson made the remarks in response to a media question about the meeting, which was held on Sept. 30 and Oct. 1 in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, the United States. Members exchanged views on issues proposed by the U.S. G20 presidency, including opposing the weaponization of food, addressing overcapacity, eliminating forced labor, and adjusting the Most-Favored-Nation (MFN) principle. Members reached a joint statement opposing the weaponization of food, while no outcome documents were issued on the remaining matters, according to the ministry. During the meeting, the Chinese side consistently upheld an attitude of openness and cooperation, constructively participated in discussions and maintained close communication with other members, fully playing its role in promoting dialogue and cooperation, said the spokesperson. At the same time, China adhered to its principles, resolutely safeguarded the common interests of China and other developing countries, and worked to promote unity and cooperation within the G20, the ministry added. Regarding the food issue, many emerging market and developing members, including China, put forward the view that food-importing and food-exporting countries should jointly safeguard the stability of food supply chains, and that all parties have the right to take measures for domestic public policy objectives and to safeguard food security, the spokesperson said. The presidency gave positive consideration to these views, which were also fully reflected in the joint statement, the spokesperson said, adding that the outcome was the result of consensus-building and the joint efforts of all G20 members. Issues such as overcapacity and forced labor were highly controversial from the outset, said the ministry. The ministry said that at present, G20 members are generally subject to additional Section 301 tariffs under the pretext of so-called "forced labor" and are mostly targets of Section 301 investigations over the so-called "overcapacity" issue. Against this backdrop, many members put forward different views on the issues set by the presidency, and the meeting ultimately failed to produce outcome documents on these matters, the ministry said. The spokesperson also noted that, after the meeting, the U.S. side issued a chair's statement mentioning that it had released a statement on forced labor with two other G20 countries outside the G20 framework. On the issue of reforming the MFN treatment principle, the vast majority of members, including China, emphasized that the principle is the cornerstone of the multilateral trading system, providing stability and predictability for global trade, and that any undermining of this principle would seriously damage the foundation of the multilateral trading system, said the ministry. In light of the views expressed by the members, the presidency did not propose an outcome document on this topic, the ministry revealed. Looking ahead to the G20 Leaders' Summit in December 2026, the spokesperson said that China is ready to work with the G20 presidency and all members to uphold consensus-building, and jointly contribute positive and practical economic and trade outcomes to the summit. item.title: China's holiday consumption market posts steady growth
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
China's holiday consumption market posts steady growth Tourists interact with actors at Yangliuqing ancient town in Tianjin, north China, Oct. 3, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Ran) BEIJING, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- Consumer spending across China is holding steady midway through the seven-day National Day holiday, with early data pointing to stable growth that reflects the economy's underlying vitality. In the first three days of the holiday from Oct. 1 to 3, foot traffic and revenue at 78 major shopping streets and commercial districts monitored by the Ministry of Commerce rose 3.4 percent and 5.3 percent year on year, respectively. Notably, the government's consumer goods trade-in program drove 19.63 billion yuan (about 2.91 billion U.S. dollars) in sales over the same period, benefiting 3.48 million consumers. In breakdown, the program drove trade-ins of 46,000 vehicles, generating 7.45 billion yuan in new car sales, along with 1.51 million home appliances worth 6.5 billion yuan and 1.71 million digital and smart devices worth 4.9 billion yuan. The National Day holiday has long been one of China's peak periods for travel, tourism and spending. Authorities had projected 2.13 billion cross-regional passenger trips in total over the seven days, averaging 300 million a day. Previous data have suggested demand remains strong as railway passenger trips on Oct. 1 alone reached 25.2 million, a single-day record. To meet surging demand, China has added train services on busy routes and waived highway tolls for private cars during the holiday. Moreover, the Ministry of Culture and Tourism launched a month-long national tourism promotion campaign in late September. Local governments are hosting more than 20,000 events spanning scenic trips, autumn outings, red tourism, study tours, night activities and local food to boost diverse premium tourism offerings, while also handing out some 310 million yuan in consumer vouchers and subsidies over the month as a way to spur tourism consumption. item.title: China's new generation shines at Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
China's new generation shines at Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games Players of China celebrate after winning the men's 3rd place match of Football between China and Uzbekistan at 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Toyota of Aichi Prefecture, Japan, Oct. 3, 2026. (Xinhua/Jia Haocheng) NAGOYA, Japan, Oct. 4 (Xinhua) -- The Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games came to a close Sunday, with China topping the gold medal table for the 12th consecutive edition, and finishing with 169 gold, 89 silver and 83 bronze medals, its best haul at an overseas Asiad. Beyond the medal count, the Games offered a glimpse of the next generation of Chinese athletes. Young competitors rose up across a spectrum of sports -- strengthening China's traditional powerhouses, breaking new ground in emerging disciplines and signaling ambitions that extend well beyond Nagoya. DEPTH ON DISPLAY China's dominance in its traditional strength events was evident throughout the Games. Chen Yuxi of China, gold medalist of the women's 10m platform and women's synchronised 10m platform, poses for photos after diving competition at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Tokyo, Japan, Sept. 30, 2026. (Xinhua/Chen Zeguo) Diving once again provided the clearest example. With Lian Junjie winning the men's 10m platform title, China swept all 10 diving gold medals on offer at the Games. Since making its Asiad debut in 1974, China has never missed out on a diving gold medal, and the latest title was the team's 100th diving gold in Asian Games history. That dominance extended across the water. Chinese swimmers won 30 gold, 13 silver and 11 bronze medals, their best-ever haul at the Games. They also swept all seven relay titles for the first time, while setting five Asian records and 17 Games records. On the track and field, China continued to turn depth into medals. The team won 17 gold, 14 silver and eight bronze medals, its best show at an Asiad held outside China since Bangkok 1998, to finish atop the athletics medal table. Shi Junhao, Liu Guoyi, Chen Yujie and Chen Jinfeng (L to R) of team China celebrate after the 4x100m relay mixed final of Athletics at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Nagoya, Japan, Sept. 29, 2026. (Xinhua/Lui Siu Wai) The momentum also extended to other medal-rich events. China claimed 16 of the overall 28 shooting titles and set five world records. "The Asiad gave us an opportunity to test our preparations for Los Angeles 2028," said Wang Lian, an official with China's shooting and archery administration. "It was also an important step in developing our team, particularly our promising young athletes." Weightlifting and gymnastics further underscored China's strength in established events. Yang Liuyue broke world records in the snatch and total in the women's 61kg category, while the men's gymnastics team captured its 13th consecutive Games title and the women's team extended its winning streak to 14 editions. Yang Liuyue of China competes during the women's 61kg final of Weightlifting at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Nagoya, Japan, Sept. 25, 2026. (Xinhua/Yu Yang) YOUTH TAKES FLIGHT China's delegation had a distinctly youthful look at the Asiad. Of its 815 athletes, 548 were making their Asian Games debuts, while 27 percent were born in 2005 or later. In the women's 400m individual medley, 13-year-old Yu Zidi and 15-year-old Ke Wenxi took gold and silver. Yu won three golds, setting Asian Games records in the 200m butterfly and 400m individual medley, as well as an Asian record in the 200m individual medley. Her performances earned her the women's Most Valuable Player award, announced by the Olympic Council of Asia on Sunday. They arrived with talent, but talent alone was not enough. Behind their breakthroughs were years of repetition, training and persistence. Yu Zidi (R) and Ke Wenxi of China react after the women's 400m individual medley final at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Tokyo, Japan, Sept. 23, 2026. (Xinhua/Wu Zhizun) "Only I know how much I went through this year. But I got through it all. I hope I can keep getting better and better," Yu said. 19-year-old Zhang Zhanshuo won seven gold medals, the most of any athlete at the Games. His celebration of counting the golds on his fingers in the pool became one of the memorable images. That confidence was on display in the field, too. 18-year-old javelin thrower Yan Ziyi made an immediate impact, launching 70.46 meters with her first attempt to improve the Games record by 4.37 meters. Yan Ziyi of China competes during the women's javelin throw final of Athletics at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Nagoya, Japan, Sept. 27, 2026. (Xinhua/Luo Yuan) "I plan to save my chance to break the world record for the 2027 World Championships in Beijing," Yan said. The emergence of young athletes such as teenage sprinter Chen Yujie offers a glimpse of what could lie ahead for Asian athletics. The 17-year-old competed in four events and won three golds and a silver, including a gold in the women's 100m in a Games-record 11.06 seconds. Off the track, her confidence was just as striking. A photo that she took a nap in the athletes' lounge before the final became a hit on Chinese social media. Chen Yujie of China celebrates after winning the women's 100m final of Athletics at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Nagoya, Japan, Sept. 25, 2026. (Xinhua/Lui Siu Wai) "These Asian Games have given me a lot of motivation. Now that it's over, I'm already looking ahead to the next challenge," Chen said. "I hope that one day I can represent China and Asian women on the world stage and showcase our strength at the Olympics." BREAKING NEW GROUND Young athletes are opening up new possibilities for Chinese sports. After years of struggling to regain the footing, China's men's football team beat Uzbekistan in a penalty shootout on Saturday to win a bronze medal, its first in 28 years at the Games. The result gave Chinese fans something more to celebrate during the National Day holiday. "This is the most valuable medal of my career," said 21-year-old center back Peng Xiao. "But I would rather see it as a starting point. I hope the generation that comes after us can one day stand higher on the podium." As the Olympic program embraces younger, more urban sports, skateboarding, sport climbing, surfing and BMX freestyle have become regular features at the Asian Games. Chinese athletes are making their mark in these events, chasing results while gaining recognition on the world stage. China's climbers made their presence felt on National Day, sweeping the women's boulder and men's speed titles to claim the country's first Asian Games gold medals in Olympic events. With Olympic and world champions in the field, both victories were hard-earned. Yang Siqi of China competes during the women's shortboard gold medal match of Surfing against Ikeda Mirai of Japan at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Tahara of Aichi Prefecture, Japan, Sept. 29, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Haobo) For 17-year-old Yang Siqi, reaching the Asiad surfing final and winning women's shortboard silver turned what once seemed out of reach into reality. The teenager from the mountainous region of southwestern China secured the country's first Asian Games surfing medal. Her dedication in training even caught the attention of Song Min, a coach with South Korea's surfing team, who said he believed Yang could one day make it to the Olympics. "I have never been afraid of surfing since I first started," Yang said. "The next step is to keep improving, one step at a time." China's skateboarders also came out on top against the host nation Japan, taking gold and bronze in the women's street event with composed performances when it mattered most. Sun Sibei of China competes during the women's park final of Cycling BMX Freestyle at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Nagoya, Japan, Sept. 27, 2026. (Xinhua/Deng Hua) 21-year-old Sun Sibei made history by winning China's first gold in the cycling BMX freestyle, which made its Asian Games debut. "I hope this niche sport can reach a wider audience, so more people can see the twists and turns in the air, and more children can have the chance to try BMX at facilities close to home," Sun said. The younger athletes are telling a different story, a story of confidence, exploration and willingness to step into unfamiliar territory. To some extent, these Games left behind more than medals: they opened up a new path for Chinese sport. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: Longer trips, richer experiences: China's National Day holiday reveals shifting tourism trends
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
Longer trips, richer experiences: China's National Day holiday reveals shifting tourism trends BEIJING, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- Five days into China's week-long National Day holiday, millions are still immersed in the sights, sounds and flavors of the season -- traveling, dining, exploring and enjoying the break. Yet this year, the scenes are subtly different. Travelers have ventured farther as the Mid-Autumn Festival holiday fell just three days before the National Day holiday, while family trips and experience-oriented travel are on the rise, according to travel agencies. "It points to a fundamental shift in the logic of tourism consumption, as travelers focus more on the quality of time and the richness of their experiences," said Bu Xiting, a researcher with the Communication University of China. LONGER BREAKS, RICHER CHOICES Data from Chinese online travel platform Tuniu shows that tours of 10 days or more are particularly popular during this holiday period, accounting for 26 percent of bookings. Yuan You, an internet company employee, spent three days of her 13-day break in Jiuzhaigou, southwest China's Sichuan Province, before heading to the provincial capital Chengdu for woodworking classes. "The holiday is rich while maintaining a relaxed pace," she said. Authorities across the country have rolled out a wide range of activities, consumer vouchers and subsidies to spur holiday spending. Shanghai, for example, has launched about 200 major consumption events, backed by consumer vouchers worth roughly 100 million yuan (around 14.85 million U.S. dollars). The offerings range from watching films and dining to purchasing digital products and cars, encouraging consumers to explore a broader spectrum of spending experiences. Cultural institutions, too, are broadening the ways people can experience and consume culture. The Sichuan Museum extended its holiday hours and launched a themed night tour, while Beijing's Zhongshan Park brought museums, cultural institutions and innovative brands together to create a market street featuring culture-inspired products. As more new energy vehicles hit the roads during the holiday, authorities have taken measures to ensure adequate charging facilities and convenient services. During last year's eight-day Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day holiday period, Chinese travelers made 888 million domestic trips and spent a combined 809 billion yuan, according to the Ministry of Culture and Tourism. This year, data shows that foot traffic and revenue at 78 major shopping streets and commercial districts monitored by the Ministry of Commerce rose 3.4 percent and 5.3 percent year on year, respectively, from Oct. 1 to 3. RED TOURISM, ROBOTS AND RURAL EXPERIENCES As China marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March, former revolutionary base areas have drawn renewed interest from holidaymakers, with visits offering travelers a chance to learn about the country's revolutionary history and reflect on the difficult years that helped shape modern China. In Yan'an, northwest China's Shaanxi Province, a street has staged special activities including performances of songs from the revolutionary years and a large-scale bonfire gathering. Visitor numbers on the first day of the holiday rose about 20 percent year on year. The holiday has also turned some of China's newest robots into part of the consumer experience, putting embodied intelligence to work alongside traditional culture in tourist attractions, shopping districts and ancient towns. At a cultural district in Chengdu, robots performed dances inspired by local opera's face-changing art and used digital technology to recreate tanghua, a traditional form of sugar painting. On Chunxi Road, a humanoid robot has gone beyond entertainment to take on the role of a store manager, greeting customers and recommending products rather than simply performing for them. China's growing network of robot training bases is preparing more machines for roles beyond the factory floor -- and beyond the country's borders. In the first half of 2026, Chinese manufacturers accounted for 97 percent of humanoid robot shipments worldwide, according to a report released at the 2026 World Robot Conference. Years of efforts to restore the environment and revitalize rural areas are also paying off. On a ridge overlooking the Miyun Reservoir in Beijing, visitors can hike to a viewing platform and enjoy outdoor concerts amid the pine trees. With roads, infrastructure and public services extending deeper into the countryside, some once-remote villages are emerging as new destinations for holidaymakers. Caijiagou, a former impoverished hillside village in east China's Shandong Province, has transformed into an art-themed destination, with murals adorning residential walls. Village official Liang Yunhui said the village has repurposed idle rural homes into cultural spaces such as an art gallery and a musical instrument museum, while hosting events featuring traditional crafts, cultural fairs and folk music. "In total, we have received more than 500,000 visits over the years," he said. On travel platform Fliggy, the number of users purchasing travel products featuring natural scenery and villages surged by nearly 50 percent from the same holiday period last year. "More travelers are seeking immersive experiences, from sampling local cuisine and making intangible cultural heritage crafts to watching distinctive performances, allowing them to gain a deeper appreciation of local culture," said a manager with Tuniu. CHINA HAUL While many Chinese tourists are venturing farther around the world, more international travelers are flocking to China to experience the country for themselves, riding a rising wave of global fascination with everything from the scenery and culture to its lifestyles and, more recently, Chinese brands and design. Tennis star Novak Djokovic, in Beijing for the China Open, was seen trying his hand at Chinese calligraphy at the Summer Palace, a former imperial garden. After a match, he used a traditional Chinese seal to put his mark on fans' keepsakes instead of signing autographs. Huaqiangbei, a sprawling electronics marketplace in south China's tech hub Shenzhen, has become a magnet for foreign shoppers looking to experience China's tech scene firsthand. Bryan Lamothe-Arice from the United States was browsing smart devices. "I'm particularly interested in the electric bikes and all kinds of flying devices here. I'm going to tell my friends to come here. There are tech products everywhere." China's border crossings are expected to see about 2.15 million passenger trips a day on average during the National Day holiday, according to the National Immigration Administration. That growing international interest is also showing up in spending. Overseas visitors spent 263.6 billion yuan in China in the first seven months of 2026, up 27.8 percent year on year, according to the commerce ministry. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. item.title: Extended breaks, richer experiences add momentum to China's holiday travel boom
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-04
Extended breaks, richer experiences add momentum to China's holiday travel boom Tourists interact with actors at Yangliuqing ancient town in Tianjin, north China, Oct. 3, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Ran) BEIJING, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- China's National Day travel market kicked off on a strong note, as many travelers linked the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day breaks with their annual leave. This trend has led to longer trips and a surge in bookings for long-haul journeys, multi-city itineraries and experience-based travel products. LONGER BREAKS, FARTHER JOURNEYS With the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day separated by only three working days this year, some travelers used three days of leave to link the two breaks into a 13-day holiday. Trip.com Group data showed that one in every 10 travelers combined the two holidays into an extended break. Cao Shuai, CEO of Tongcheng Travel's destination business division, said strong demand for the 13-day break has lengthened the overall consumption cycle and helped release demand for long-haul and in-depth travel. Data from online travel platform Qunar showed that by Oct. 1, the first day of the National Day holiday, 20 percent of travelers had already reached the second city on their itineraries. Nearly 30 percent had booked hotels in at least two cities, while bookings involving stays in four or more cities surged 53 percent year on year. For Yuan You, who works for an internet company, the 13-day break made it possible to split one holiday into two distinct stages. She planned to first spend three days in Jiuzhaigou, a UNESCO-listed scenic area in southwest China's Sichuan Province known for its turquoise lakes and waterfalls, before continuing to Chengdu for the remainder of the break. "With such a long break, spending the whole time either resting or sightseeing can become monotonous, so I opted for a mix of both," Yuan said. In Chengdu, she chose to spend part of that extra time learning woodworking. Longer breaks are encouraging people to travel farther. Flight bookings for journeys of more than 2,000 km rose 76 percent year on year during the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day period, accounting for more than a quarter of all flight bookings, according to Meituan. Wang Peng, an associate researcher at the Beijing Academy of Social Sciences, said the extended break has encouraged more people to start traveling earlier, spreading trips over a longer period rather than concentrating them within a few peak days. That, Wang said, could help sustain demand across tourism, accommodation and catering services for longer periods of time. Passengers walk out of Nanjing Railway Station in Nanjing, east China's Jiangsu Province, Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo by Su Yang/Xinhua) China State Railway Group Co., Ltd. (China Railway) said that China's railway network handled 25.204 million passenger trips on Oct. 1, setting a new single-day record. RICHER EXPERIENCES, MORE TO EXPLORE The surge in mobility has translated into demand for richer experiences at destinations. At the National Maritime Museum of China in north China's Tianjin Municipality, 19,000 visitors streamed through the doors on the opening day of the National Day break. Among the new draws is "Echoes of the Whale Song," the museum's first customized full-sensory virtual reality experience. Unlike conventional walk-through VR attractions, visitors remain seated as the experience unfolds around them, allowing for a more immersive encounter. Under blue lights, visitors see a giant whale entangled in discarded fishing nets and take part in a virtual rescue, learning along the way about the impact of marine debris on ocean life. Such experience-oriented products are gaining traction well beyond one museum. On Fliggy, Alibaba Group's online travel platform, domestic attraction ticket bookings on Oct. 1 rose nearly 30 percent year on year, while the number of users purchasing products for natural scenic areas and villages increased by nearly 50 percent. Tourists watch an immersive drama at the former site of L'indo Bank of China in Tianjin, north China, Sept. 27, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhao Zishuo) Searches on Qunar for "immersive performances," "fireworks shows" and "night tours" also climbed more than 50 percent year on year. The growing demand for interactive travel experiences can be seen at Changchun Zoological and Botanical Park in northeast China's Jilin Province. There, a nighttime immersive show inspired by the Chinese classic "Journey to the West" has drawn large crowds into a vibrant fantasy world, with costumed performers mingling with visitors and transforming the park into a stage after dark. Yang Han, a researcher with Qunar's big data research institute, said travelers are increasingly setting out to "enter a story" rather than simply view static scenery, with content-driven experiences gaining popularity and bringing new opportunities to less traditional tourism destinations. Bu Xiting, an associate researcher in the School of Cultural Industries Management at Communication University of China, contrasted the current trend with the previously popular "special forces-style tourism," a fast-paced form of travel in which people try to pack as many sights as possible into a short period, and city walks, which offer smaller-scale urban experiences during pockets of free time. By linking public holidays with annual leave, travelers now have more time to shape their trips around what they want to experience, Bu said. Tourism consumption, Bu noted, is shifting from a focus on "time efficiency" toward greater "experience density." item.title: Beyond mining tunnels: China's coal-rich province accelerates smarter, greener energy transition
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-04
Beyond mining tunnels: China's coal-rich province accelerates smarter, greener energy transition This photo taken on Sept. 4, 2026 shows a view outside the main venue of the 2026 Taiyuan Energy Low-Carbon Development Forum in Taiyuan, north China's Shanxi Province. (Xinhua/Yang Chenguang) TAIYUAN, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- From intelligent coal mines to digital power-grid management, north China's Shanxi Province is accelerating its energy transition and maintaining stable coal supplies. As one of China's major coal-producing provinces and a key national energy base, Shanxi is seeking to make its energy system smarter, more diversified and more efficient. The province is upgrading its traditional coal industry through smarter technologies and cleaner production, while expanding wind and solar power to diversify its energy mix. Backed by increasingly flexible power management, these efforts are reshaping how Shanxi produces, supplies and uses energy as China pursues greener development. AUTOMATED COAL MINING For 50-year-old Zhao Huacheng, deputy head of a fully mechanized mining team at Huayang New Material Technology Group Co., Ltd., a major coal mining enterprise in Shanxi, the transformation of coal mining is evident in his daily work. Zhao has worked in the industry for nearly 30 years, taking on almost every frontline role in his team, from coal miner and powered-support operator to safety officer. Huayang's No. 1 Mine, with an annual production capacity of 8.5 million tonnes, is among China's first batch of intelligent demonstration coal mines. Its intelligent mining faces use 5G technology and automated equipment to enable remote control and reduce the need for underground workers. The number of workers required underground for a shift at Zhao's team has already fallen from 24 to 16. Operating a coal-cutting machine was once one of the toughest jobs. Three operators had to work together, with one controlling the machine from a platform and the other two observing the terrain from the front and rear. When the machine started up, clouds of coal dust often made it nearly impossible to see, and flying chunks of coal posed a real risk of injury. Zhao still has a scar near his right eye as a reminder. "With advances in technology, the operator in the middle is no longer needed. The operators in front and behind can control the machine remotely from six meters away, reducing the risks," Zhao said. "We used to get bumped and bruised almost constantly. Now, such incidents are rare." Today, intelligent equipment has taken over most labor-intensive tasks. Clean mine tunnels, dust-suppression systems and enclosed control rooms have replaced the once dusty and hazardous working conditions. Productivity has also seen a sharp increase. A production shift that once yielded about 3,000 to 4,000 tonnes of coal can now produce 5,000 to 6,000 tonnes, according to Zhao. The transformation at Zhao's workplace is part of a broader push to make coal mining smarter and cleaner in Shanxi. By the end of November 2025, the province had built 369 intelligent coal mines, accounting for more than one-third of the national total, as well as 75 demonstration mines for green mining. On the national level, China aims to make virtually all types of coal mines intelligent by 2035 by leveraging advanced technologies, according to the National Development and Reform Commission. DIVERSIFIED ENERGY SUPPLY While making coal production smarter and cleaner, Shanxi is also reshaping its energy mix, with renewable energy becoming an increasingly important source of new capacity and power generation. At Shanxi Jinnan Steel Group Co., Ltd. in Quwo County, Linfen City, photovoltaic panels cover unused spaces ranging from rooftops and south-facing walls to hillside slopes and areas near an artificial lake. The company produces nearly 6 million tonnes of steel annually. Over the past five years, it has invested heavily in clean energy projects to reduce the carbon intensity of its energy consumption. Three months ago, the company partnered with PowerChina New Energy Group Co., Ltd. to develop green electricity by tapping the region's mountainous and valley resources. The two sides plan to use a "green electricity direct supply" model to better match the company's energy needs. "We have developed photovoltaic projects with a combined capacity of 550 megawatts, generating more than 1 billion kWh of electricity annually," said Zhang Tianfu, president of Shanxi Jinnan Steel Group Co., Ltd. Green electricity currently accounts for 15 percent of the company's power consumption. Zhang said the company will continue expanding its renewable energy portfolio and plans to raise the share to 50 percent by 2029. The company's growing investment in green electricity comes as renewable energy has become the main source of newly added power generation capacity and electricity generation in Shanxi. By the end of June this year, the province's installed capacity of wind and solar power had exceeded 80 million kW. In 2020, roughly one in every seven kWh generated in Shanxi came from renewable sources. Today, despite a substantial increase in total power generation, the share has risen to one in every four kWh. A historic shift has taken place in Shanxi's energy mix. By the end of September last year, installed capacity of new and clean energy sources accounted for 54.55 percent of the province's total, marking a historic shift from a fossil-fuel-dominated energy mix toward one led by clean energy. SMARTER POWER MANAGEMENT As wind and solar power generation expands, Shanxi faces a new challenge: how to accommodate increasingly variable renewable generation while keeping the power grid stable. Virtual power plants are emerging as one solution. Shanxi Fengxingcekong Co., Ltd. operates China's first virtual power plant participating in the electricity spot market. Nan Dou, deputy general manager of the company, said the spot market generates a new electricity price every five minutes. The virtual power plant aggregates scattered electricity-consuming resources and dispatches them through a digital platform, using algorithms to adjust the power loads of participating enterprises in response to changes in electricity prices and grid demand. "When electricity prices are low and renewable power generation is high, we encourage enterprises to consume more electricity, maximizing the use of renewable power. When prices are high and the grid is under pressure, we organize enterprises to reduce their loads during peak periods, helping ensure safe and stable grid operation," Nan said. "This benefits all three sides by ensuring power supplies, facilitating renewable power consumption and reducing energy costs for enterprises," he added. From August 2023 to June 2026, the virtual power plant helped facilitate the consumption of 350 million kWh of renewable electricity, equivalent to reducing carbon dioxide emissions by about 350,000 tonnes, the operators said. It also saved about 210 million kWh of electricity. Over the three years since entering the electricity market, the company's ability to aggregate and dispatch resources has continued to improve. The number of users on its platform has risen from five to more than 60, while its aggregated capacity has jumped from 80,000 kW to 2.282 million kW. "The most important improvement is that our control success rate has risen from 33 percent to 80 percent. Only by improving the quality of regulation can we achieve the desired results," Nan said. As of September 2026, 14 virtual power plants in Shanxi had participated in market trading, aggregating 1,459 users. Their combined capacity in the Shanxi electricity market had reached 6.4548 million kW, with a maximum adjustable load of 1.545 million kW. Traditional coal-fired power plants are also undergoing flexibility upgrades in response to market signals. The upgrades allow them to reduce output when wind and solar generation is abundant, creating more room for renewable power, and quickly ramp up output when renewable generation falls short, helping ensure electricity supplies. More than half of Shanxi's coal-fired power generating units have completed such flexibility upgrades. "Guided by market needs, Shanxi's renewable electricity utilization rate has remained above 90 percent," said Zhang Chao, an official in charge of the spot market at the Dispatching and Control Center of State Grid Shanxi Electric Power Co., Ltd. item.title: New paths to lower carbon take shape on China's tropical island
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-04
New paths to lower carbon take shape on China's tropical island A drone photo shows cruises sailing near the Phoenix Island in Sanya, south China's Hainan Province, Oct. 3, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhao Yingquan) HAIKOU, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- With a gentle pull of a lever, an operator sends a giant claw plunging into a mountain of waste at a waste-to-energy plant. It scoops up more than five tonnes at a time -- enough to generate the electricity a typical household uses in a year. The waste is then fed into incinerators burning at over 850 degrees Celsius. The plant in China's southernmost province of Hainan processes some 4,200 tonnes of household garbage daily, generating about 1.7 million kilowatt-hours of power, roughly what more than 200,000 households use in a day. This transformation of trash into energy is part of a broader low-carbon experiment in Hainan, known for its blue seas, tropical forests and abundant sunshine. Since 2021, Hainan has closed 16 household waste landfills. With eight waste-to-energy plants now in operation, the province has achieved zero landfilling of untreated household waste, saving precious land resources while reducing the emission of methane, a potent greenhouse gas, generated by landfills. However, disposing of waste in a more environmentally friendly way is only part of the story. Hainan is also working to reduce waste at its source, beginning with plastic bags. The change can be seen at a produce market in the provincial capital Haikou. Each of the more than 300 stalls has a digital ledger tracking where their shopping bags were bought, while a system generates green, yellow or red codes daily to flag whether the bags meet environmental requirements. Since the digital system was introduced in April, the use of fully biodegradable bags has jumped from 18 percent to 81 percent in the market. Staff members demonstrate the procedure of plastic recycling in the Boao zero-carbon demonstration zone in Boao, south China's Hainan Province, March 25, 2025. (Xinhua/Xie Ziyi) The call for biodegradable bags at the market was initially met with skepticism, with some vendors even hiding non-compliant bags from inspectors. A meat vendor surnamed Wu, who has worked at the market for seven years, was among the skeptics, assuming that greener bags would simply cost more. "Only after comparing them did I realize that the biodegradable bags here are cheaper than those sold elsewhere or online, and they are more durable," Wu said. The market is one small piece of a province-wide push. Hainan was the first in China to impose a province-wide ban on non-biodegradable single-use plastic products through legislation. By the end of 2025, alternatives to such banned plastic products accounted for an average of 80.2 percent at key venues including schools, hospitals, supermarkets and produce markets. "A 'zero-waste island' is not simply about waste management, but a green transition that runs through the entire operation of a city," said Wang Chenye, deputy head of the Hainan academy of environmental sciences. Some 100 km away from Haikou, a low-carbon experiment is also underway in the town of Boao. The Boao zero-carbon demonstration zone, China's first project to achieve zero-carbon operation through urban renewal, was created by retrofitting an existing area rather than being built from scratch. Inside a hotel kitchen on Boao's Dongyu Island, chefs toss woks over sizzling stoves, but there is no flame in sight. Hotel kitchens across the island have been fully electrified. "An all-electric kitchen alone can cut carbon dioxide emissions by 7.5 tonnes a day," said Luo Hu, an engineer with COSCO SHIPPING Boao Co., Ltd., a company involved in the zero-carbon demonstration zone project. He added that carbon traceability has been introduced for one-fifth of the dishes to help diners better understand the carbon footprint. Across Dongyu Island in Boao, hotels and conference venues have undergone green renovations, while vehicles and boats have switched to new energy. Altogether, the transformation involved 18 projects spanning green buildings, renewable energy and greener transport, according to Luo. An aerial drone photo taken on March 16, 2025 shows the photovoltaic devices on the roof of the Boao Forum for Asia (BFA) International Conference Center and a BFA hotel in the Boao zero-carbon demonstration zone in Boao, south China's Hainan Province. (Xinhua/Pu Xiaoxu) "Carrying out zero-carbon retrofits with high heat, high humidity and frequent typhoons means there is no ready-made model to follow," said Zeng Youwen, chief engineer of the Hainan branch of the China Academy of Urban Planning and Design. The effort has paid off. The zone now generates more green electricity than it consumes and has entered sustained zero-carbon operation. Energy-related carbon dioxide emissions from buildings and municipal infrastructure in the zone fell from about 11,350 tonnes in 2019 to just 14.6 tonnes in 2025, a reduction of 99.9 percent. Hainan is seeking to take such low-carbon practices much further during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030). Under a provincial low-carbon island plan, Hainan aims to complete building a low-carbon island before 2045 and reduce annual CO2 emissions by 70 percent from peak levels. The plan maps out changes across energy, industry, transport and buildings, alongside efforts to strengthen the island's carbon sinks. The pursuit is already yielding tangible results in Hegui Village in Lingao County. Some 48 hectares of mangroves, long valued for shielding the coast from waves, are estimated to sequester 3,236.05 tonnes of carbon over seven years, potentially bringing over 320,000 yuan (about 47,500 U.S. dollars) to the village collective. "This mangrove forest not only protects us from waves, but earns money through carbon credits," said Chen Hongwei, an official of the village. "That gives us even more reason to protect it." item.title: A taste of home in orbit: How China keeps its astronauts well-fed
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-04
A taste of home in orbit: How China keeps its astronauts well-fed This image captured at Beijing Aerospace Control Center on May 25, 2026 shows a group picture of the crew of Shenzhou-21 and Shenzhou-23 spaceships. (Xinhua/Jin Liwang) BEIJING, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- Although called Tiangong, or "Heavenly Palace," China's space station is becoming less distant and more like home, as astronauts bring the comforting tastes into orbit. The Chinese space kitchen now serves nearly 200 food items. Alongside dumplings and mooncakes, home-style dishes such as Kung Pao chicken, mapo tofu and fried rice have made it onto the station's menu. Videos showing astronauts savoring freshly cooked meat and cakes in orbit have gone viral. Their smiling faces and bright eyes make the aroma almost leap off the screen. Yang Liwei, the country's first astronaut, joked at a recent press conference that he was envious. He said astronauts can now use air-frying equipment in space and enjoy baked chicken wings in orbit. During his Shenzhou-5 mission in 2003, which lasted less than one day, his diet was limited to packaged instant food that could not be heated. Microgravity, cosmic radiation and the enclosed cabin environment impose strict requirements on space diets. Floating particles and droplets may drift into instruments and trigger malfunctions. Since Yuri Gagarin, the first human to travel into space, paste-like food and compressed energy bars had long served as the standard meals for astronauts. In June 2013, Wang Yaping, together with two fellow male crewmates, carried out the 15-day Shenzhou-10 space mission. People remembered this female astronaut with a ponytail for her space lecture. At the same time, the image of her floating a "zongzi," a leaf-wrapped rice dumpling, by hand also left a deep impression on the public. Zongzi is traditionally enjoyed during the Dragon Boat Festival, which happened to coincide with the Shenzhou-10 mission that year. To help the astronauts celebrate, this special snack was added to the spaceship pantry. Students watch Wang Yaping (R) demonstrating drinking water in China's space station, at the China Science and Technology Museum in Beijing, capital of China, Dec. 9, 2021. (Xinhua/Jin Liwang) Eight years later, Wang spent Spring Festival aboard the Tiangong space station during the Shenzhou-13 mission. It is also China's first six-month-long space stay. Scientists customized the cuisine: for instance, they prepared dumplings with seafood fillings because Wang grew up by the sea, and plenty of spicy food for crew member Ye Guangfu, who was born in chili-obsessed Sichuan Province. At that time, the core module Tianhe had several sections, including those for working, sleeping, dining and exercising. The videos of Shenzhou-13 crew practicing calligraphy and playing Taichi became social media hits. China completed the construction of its space station in 2022, with one core module and two lab modules forming a 110-square-meter orbital structure. Oxygen can be fully regenerated, and water recovery exceeds 95 percent. Since then, long-duration spaceflights have become routine, and the Chinese "space home" can host up to six astronauts in orbit at a time. Space residency is also set to last even longer. One member of the Shenzhou-23 crew, currently aboard the Tiangong, will conduct a one-year in-orbit stay. Moreover, as China pushes further into deep-space exploration, these extended stays will become the norm, which means astronauts' diets will be more important than ever. This screen image captured at Beijing Aerospace Control Center on April 16, 2026 shows Shenzhou-21 astronaut Wu Fei performing extravehicular activities outside China's orbiting space station.(Photo by Zhang Fan/Xinhua) Because weightlessness causes bone calcium loss and muscle atrophy, space food must be high in calcium and protein, low in sodium and balanced in dietary fiber. According to the Astronaut Center of China, researchers have developed space food that counteracts oxidative damage, supports immunity, reduces fatigue and regulates the gut microbiome. But taste is another problem. In microgravity, blood shifts upward, causing nasal congestion and cutting smell sensitivity by at least 30 percent. Since taste is closely tied to smell, astronauts often find food bland. The center's researchers have responded with adding more strong-flavored dishes, with liquid soy sauce and concentrated chili sauce. New technology has also played a big role in keeping astronauts well-fed. The astronaut center, in collaboration with private companies, has upgraded the "space kitchen" with a suite of intelligent appliances for drinking water, food reheating and baking. This allows astronauts in orbit to enjoy hot meals within 20 minutes, rather than waiting longer or eating cold food. Liu Weibo, an expert with the center, gave an example of the hot-air baking oven, which is a pioneering Chinese design for space use that can efficiently remove cooking fumes and allow astronauts to enjoy barbecue in orbit. During a space lecture for Hong Kong and Macao students last month, Shenzhou-23 crew member Li Jiaying, or Lai Ka-ying in Cantonese, showed freshly baked cakes and said they reminded her of egg waffles, a popular snack from her hometown. She is a Hong Kong local. Students attend a live space lecture of the "Tiangong Class" Hong Kong and Macao Designated Session in Hong Kong, south China, Sept. 9, 2026.(Photo by Lui Sui Wai/Xinhua) Space food supplies have also become more diverse and nutritious, including more fruits and vegetables, as well as frozen steak and chicken wings. The next-generation cargo craft Qingzhou, designed for future in-orbit supply delivery, will have greater cold-chain transport capacity. However, long-term space residency requires reducing dependence on Earth's supplies, said center expert Bian Qiang. "The controlled ecological life-support tests we are conducting are intended to build an ecosystem in space that regenerates water, air and food on site, to reduce extraterrestrial survival's dependence on Earth resupply and ultimately achieve self-sufficiency." Since the Shenzhou-16 mission in 2023, China has been growing plants in orbit. It has tested more than 20 varieties from 14 plant species, including lettuce, carrots, potatoes and wheat. The Shenzhou-18 crew in 2024 was tasked with raising fish in an "aquarium" to study how space affects their growth. Scientists said the work may one day allow astronauts to enjoy fish from their own in-orbit harvests. Photo taken on Feb. 26, 2021 shows sprouting rice seeds that had made a round trip to the moon aboard the Chang'e-5 probe at the central greenhouse of the National Engineering Research Center of Plant Space Breeding of the South China Agricultural University in Guangzhou of south China's Guangdong Province. (Xinhua/Liu Dawei) China is targeting a crewed lunar landing by 2030. Living on the moon will make resupply much more challenging because of the increased distance from Earth. "We plan to build a Chinese 'lunar vegetable garden' on the moon," Bian said. From heating, baking to farming, feeding astronauts well in space is not a luxury. It is part of the mission, bringing a taste of home to the universe. Related Stories Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.
